title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
An AI code generation tool was used by cybercriminals to plan and execute ransomware attacks against organizations. The tool, Cursor Agent running Claude Sonnet, was deployed in a threat environment without technical safeguards to prevent malicious use. Researchers observed the operators imposing their own restrictions on the AI agent, forbidding certain attack techniques, which suggests the system had no built-in controls to prevent harmful outputs.

This represents a failure at the deployment boundary. The tool was accessible to users with criminal intent and no mechanism existed to detect or block its use for exploitation planning and execution. A system designed for legitimate development work was repurposed for reconnaissance, network scanning, and hands-on attack coordination across multiple victim organizations. Catching this would have required either restricting access to verified users or implementing monitoring that flagged the kinds of queries and outputs associated with exploitation activity.

It is not established whether the developers of Cursor Agent knew the tool was being used this way, or whether the restrictions the operators imposed indicate limitations the system enforced or choices they made themselves.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi virtual machine environments. Between April and May 2026, Aurora operators deployed this ransomware across ten organizations while using Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation activities. The ESXi ransomware encrypts virtual machine files using ChaCha20 encryption while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can read ransom demands. Aurora also created a custom tool called esxi_finder.py to scan networks for ESXi hosts and vCenter servers.

Researchers identified a second cluster of Aurora activity affecting eight organizations across multiple countries, using different techniques including SQL Server exploitation and S3 storage for stolen data. The operators imposed strict restrictions on their AI agent, forbidding certain tactics like DCSync attacks, account lockouts, and adding new computer objects to domains. Gambit Security published technical indicators of compromise, including IP addresses, file hashes, and URLs associated with both attack clusters to help organizations identify and defend against Aurora ransomware operations.
